options.text: It reads the file, sees the failure, and fails the run.
options.why: Wrong. A grader that reads only the reply never sees the file; that is the trouble.

options.text: It passes some of these runs, at its false-pass rate.
options.why: Right. A judge that reads the claim believes it some of the time, and the rate is its own.

options.text: It passes every one of them, since the claim sounds confident.
options.why: Tempting. A judge can rubber-stamp most claims, but not by design every time; its rate is a property to measure.

outcome: The model grader passed some of these claims at its false-pass rate. The code check failed every one.
question: A run's reply says all checks pass and the work is done. The file still fails its check. A model grader reads only the reply. What does it do with this run?

options.text: Block only when the new interval sits fully below the old one's.
options.why: Right. A drop inside the overlap is inside the noise, so blocking on it blocks good changes.

options.text: Block on any drop, however small.
options.why: Wrong. A few points from a few trials can be pure noise.

options.text: Never block: a drop is always noise.
options.why: Wrong. A drop whose interval sits clearly below the old one is a real regression.

question: A regression eval's pass rate drops by a few points. What should CI do?

options.text: It is 62%, but it does not say which way the errors fall; count the false passes apart.
options.why: Right. The same agreement can hide many false passes or many false fails.

options.text: The grader is right 62% of the time about every kind of run.
options.why: Wrong. An agreement rate is one number over all cases; it does not describe each kind of run.

options.text: The grader's 38 misses all lean one way.
options.why: Wrong. The agreement rate does not say that; the false passes and false fails must be counted.

question: A model grader agrees with human labels on 62 of 100 cases. What does the agreement rate tell you, and what does it not?

options.text: Keep a held-out set you never tune on or show to the model.
options.why: Right. A case the model never saw cannot be remembered, so the score measures the task.

options.text: Add more tasks from the public set you tuned on.
options.why: Wrong. More cases from the same contaminated set add more memory, not more signal.

options.text: Run the same tasks twice and average them.
options.why: Wrong. Repeating contaminated tasks averages the memory, it does not remove it.

question: Which step reduces the effect of contamination on your score?

options.text: The reply says done while the file's check fails.
options.why: Right. The reply claims what the check contradicts; read it beside the file.

options.text: The model grader's pass rate is high.
options.why: Tempting. A high pass rate alone proves nothing; it must be set against the code check.
